transcription: September walks into Wall Street wearing a warning label. Barron's calls it the market's most brutal month. But when September is almost over, a nearly one-hundred-year pattern begins. It finished higher in twenty-three of twenty-four cycles. And almost every winner dropped first. To know what to expect this September, we have to separate the finish from the ride. TradeWave shows ninety-eight Septembers. Fifty-two finished lower and forty-six finished higher. That is barely worse than a coin flip. So why the terrible reputation? Because the red months hurt more. Losing Septembers fell about four and a half percent on average. Winning Septembers gained about three percent. And September nineteen thirty-one fell almost thirty percent. September does not always fall. Its bad years can simply be very bad. A monthly bar also hides the ride. TradeWave calls the biggest move up after an entry M F E, and the deepest move down M A E. In twenty-four midterm Septembers like twenty twenty-six, twenty-two traded below their starting level. Yet only thirteen finished lower, while eleven finished higher. A dip was common. A bad finish was not guaranteed. Now add politics. President Trump's approval rating is around thirty-three percent, and the midterm election is November third. Wouldn't the administration push hard to keep markets positive? It has a reason to try. But wanting a strong market is not controlling one. The White House cannot order company profits, oil prices, interest rates, or the Federal Reserve. Previous midterm years still looked a lot like September. But this year has a real argument for the bulls. August gained about two and a half percent. The index entered September up double digits for the year and above its fifty-day average. Barron's found eleven similar postwar setups. Only one had a losing September. History says bumpy. Momentum says a drop is not automatic. Watch four pressure points: jobs on September fourth, inflation on the tenth and eleventh, the Fed on the sixteenth, and options expiration on the eighteenth. Then we reach the date I care about most. TradeWave's strongest midterm window began around September twenty-seventh and ran into the following July. Twenty-three of twenty-four completed cycles finished higher. But twenty-one of those twenty-three winners first fell below their entry price. The finish was impressive. The ride was not. In the next video, I will show the one cycle that failed, the drawdowns hidden inside the winners, and what would prove - or break - this nearly one-hundred-year pattern in twenty twenty-six. For now, remember: September has been mildly negative and often uncomfortable, but it is far from automatically bearish. History is a map, not a promise.
